quote: Stelle auf eine Theorie des Rechnens d. h. ergründe worin die Vortheile bekann=
english: Set up a theory of calculation, i.e. find out wherein the advantages of the know[n] ... (continues on next page).
topic: Three short notes: proving that the Bernoulli function (polynomial) is irreducible, using its behaviour modulo a prime degree p; a remark that an ideal probability device (wheel of fortune) is impossible; and a task to set up a theory of calculation.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a precise mathematical question. It is a programmatic note: 'Set up a theory of calculation (Rechnen), i.e. find out wherein the advantages of the known [methods of calculation lie] …', and the sentence breaks off at the page boundary. Read in modern terms, it asks for a general theory of computational procedures that would explain why some known calculation methods are better than others, meaning more efficient or shorter. That is loosely like what we now call algorithm analysis or computational complexity. This page does not show the rest of the sentence or any particular algorithm or problem class.
triage.answered_by: No one answered this note as such. The only commentary I found is from the Hilbert Notebook Project (Susumu Hayashi et al.), which lists this entry as a 'Theory of calculations' note in Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600. They read it as showing Hilbert's interest in computation in mathematics and say it contains an idea 'resembling the modern concept of computational complexity'. That is their interpretation. It does not show that Hilbert developed the idea or that anyone later took it up. Computational complexity theory did grow up later, but I found no source tying it to this note.

evidence.claim: The Hilbert Notebook Project lists a 'Theory of calculations' entry in Hilbert's notebooks (Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600:1-3), beginning 'Set up a theory of calculations i.e.'. It says the note shows Hilbert's interest in computation in mathematics and that he had 'an idea resembling the modern concept of computational complexity'.

The same project puts related notes in these notebooks in the late 1880s, including an early form of the 10th problem and the 'solvability of every mathematical problem by a finite number of operations' note (dated about 1888-89). It groups the calculation note with these under 'Thoughts on computation'.
Recent historical work on Hilbert's notebooks (Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600) looks at his early ideas about decidability and mechanical calculation in connection with his problems.

triage.why: The entry is an unfinished reminder to himself to build a theory of calculation. The part that would say which 'known' methods he meant is cut off, so no specific problem can be pinned down. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Historians (Hayashi's project) have catalogued it as a computation-related note and compared it loosely to computational complexity. However, I found no source saying Hilbert or anyone else followed up this specific programme or 'answered' it. The broad field it resembles, the theory of algorithms and complexity, is very active. But this connection is only a historian's comparison, not a documented line of descent, so 'active today' for this particular note is marked unclear.
